 Feature Request
I would like to see if there's enough people who would benefit (as I think I would) from a new pair of flags in the build directive to allow users to specify one or more modules to be included / excluded during the build step dynamically and separately from the pyproject.toml definitions.

Like so: poetry build --with --without 

 Rationale
In monorepositories where one could have contextually related micro-applications (or microservices), it is currently not possible to build a distribution package without specifying what modules are part of this service dynamically.

Let's imagine we have a project that is laid out like so:

 

Our pyproject.toml has this:
 

foo is the global context, our main project name. bar and baz are component modules in this context. They are meant to become (let's pretend) lambda functions or be dockerised and run by themselves. They also need a shared library which is specific only to them and no other project in the company would ever wish to use this shared library.

Now, it stands to reason that I do not want to create three different repos for this. It also feels unreasonable to make foo_bar, foo_baz and foo_shared into their own Poetry projects, as each top-level project is not a valid Python module and therefore I could no longer do from foo_shared import config from within foo_bar as an example.

Additionally, for local development, I might want to install ALL those projects without special config, so having them all listed statically as above is very useful, however - here's where the issue is..

When I dockerise foo_bar - I make use of poetry in the build step of the docker image. Something like:

 
This ensures that in my final layer, I can simply transfer the /venv folder with the installed project and run it like - python -m my_project as an ENTRYPOINT. 

And this works well, except that in the above example, Poetry builds a single wheel and the installed project would allow one to run:
- python -m foo_bar
- python -m foo_baz
- python -m foo_shared (Although this would yell as shared is a lib not an "executable" module..)

Using this sort of setup I am able to have a single CI pipeline build all my images from a single repository and distribute them further down the chain as needed, without the need for splitting the repo up or using multiple Poetry projects.

However if build had the aforementioned flags, the command could then willingly ignore foo_baz during the build stage and the resulting wheel would only carry foo_bar and foo_shared which is all that is needed for foo_bar to work in the docker container.
It would only take this command poetry build --with foo_bar foo_shared and that's it. It would explicitly only build a wheel including those two folders.

Paired together with the already existing optional dependency groups via --with and --without, this could add to the flexibility of Poetry and allow people to have more control over how projects are built in order to suit their preferred setup.

 Caveats

I am unsure how deps would work in this context, I would assume that it would be enough to first install the project using a set of dependency groups to generate a correct lockfile which then in return would tell build that those two out of three project packages it is building into the wheel need only those deps?

## Feature Request
I would like to see if there's enough people who would benefit (as I think I would) from a new pair of flags in the `build` directive to allow users to specify one or more modules to be included / excluded during the build step dynamically and separately from the `pyproject.toml` definitions.

Like so: `poetry build --with <package_1> <package_2> --without <package_3>`

## Rationale
In monorepositories where one could have contextually related micro-applications (or microservices), it is currently not possible to build a distribution package without specifying what modules are part of this service dynamically.

Let's imagine we have a project that is laid out like so:

```
repository_root/
    ...
    foo_bar/
        ...
        __init__.py
        __main__.py
    foo_baz/
        ...
        __init__.py
        __main__.py
    foo_shared/
        ...
        __init__.py
    ...
    pyproject.toml
    Dockerfile.bar
    Dockerfile.baz
```

Our `pyproject.toml` has this:
```toml
[tool.poetry]
name = "foo"
version = "0.1.0"
...
packages = [
    { include = "foo_bar" },
    { include = "foo_baz" },
    { include = "foo_shared" }
]
```

`foo` is the global context, our main project name. `bar` and `baz` are component modules in this context. They are meant to become (let's pretend) lambda functions or be dockerised and run by themselves. They also need a shared library which is specific only to them and no other project in the company would ever wish to use this shared library.

Now, it stands to reason that I do not want to create three different repos for this. It also feels unreasonable to make `foo_bar`, `foo_baz` and `foo_shared` into their own Poetry projects, as each top-level project is not a valid Python module and therefore I could no longer do `from foo_shared import config` from within `foo_bar` as an example.

Additionally, for local development, I might want to install ALL those projects without special config, so having them all listed statically as above is very useful, however - here's where the issue is..

When I dockerise `foo_bar` - I make use of poetry in the build step of the docker image. Something like:

```Dockerfile
# Dockerfile.bar
FROM base as builder

ENV POETRY_VERSION 1.3.0
WORKDIR /builder

COPY pyproject.toml poetry.lock ./

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir "poetry==$POETRY_VERSION" \
    && python -m venv /venv \
    && poetry export --with my_dep_group -f requirements.txt | /venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r /dev/stdin

COPY . /builder

RUN poetry build && /venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir dist/*.whl
```
This ensures that in my final layer, I can simply transfer the `/venv` folder with the installed project and run it like - `python -m my_project` as an `ENTRYPOINT`. 

And this works well, except that in the above example, Poetry builds a single wheel and the installed project would allow one to run:
- `python -m foo_bar`
- `python -m foo_baz`
- `python -m foo_shared` (Although this would yell as shared is a lib not an "executable" module..)

Using this sort of setup I am able to have a single CI pipeline build all my images from a single repository and distribute them further down the chain as needed, without the need for splitting the repo up or using multiple Poetry projects.

However if `build` had the aforementioned flags, the command could then willingly ignore `foo_baz` during the build stage and the resulting wheel would only carry `foo_bar` and `foo_shared` which is all that is needed for `foo_bar` to work in the docker container.
It would only take this command `poetry build --with foo_bar foo_shared` and that's it. It would explicitly only build a wheel including those two folders.

Paired together with the already existing optional dependency groups via `--with` and `--without`, this could add to the flexibility of Poetry and allow people to have more control over how projects are built in order to suit their preferred setup.

## Caveats

I am unsure how deps would work in this context, I would assume that it would be enough to first install the project using a set of dependency groups to generate a correct lockfile which then in return would tell `build` that those two out of three project packages it is building into the wheel need only those deps?

 Feature Request

 What
I'd like an option to use lockfile dependencies in built wheel instead of pyproject.toml versions. I want to be able to build a wheel with poetry, install it with _any_ python package manager (even pip) and end up with the same dependencies as I would have through by invoking poetry install.

At the moment dependencies written into a wheel metadata are pretty much passed through from pyproject.toml (largely) unadulterated. I want an option to explicitly use the versions (and only those versions) in pyproject.lock as the dependencies of the wheel.

 Why

I'd like this so that we can clean up a fuzzy boundary between poetry being an amazing development tool _(it really is very good!)_ and a rather mediocre distribution / deployment deployment tool. This fuzzy line also makes it tricky to have a clear boundary between source and artefact in some contexts.

I don't think poetry ever tried to be a distribution / deployment tool. I don't think it was necessarily envisaged that poetry would need to be installed on the target [eg: end user's machine etc].

However this is what's happening in the wild because of one feature of poetry: the lock file. The lock file is so good that people want to keep using it downstream right onto the target machine as well. Right now the only way to do this is to copy the source onto the target machine, install poetry, and execute poetry install.

That's because at the moment the lockfile information is not embedded into the wheel. If you built the wheel and just distributed that the target environment would end up with different dependencies.

 Example use case

One concrete use case is building docker images. I don't think lockfiles were ever intended as a way to ensure that docker images contained the same dependencies as the development project.

But some of us do have a real requirement to ensure our docker images build exactly as we intended them to.

If you look through poetry issues, you'll find a good few people complaining that installing poetry in a docker image is complex and messy. _(though it has admittedly improved in versions between 1.1 to 1.3)_

 Closing remarks

I'd like to humbly suggest that poetry doesn't need to take any interest in building docker images into account. This should not generally be supported. There is a very rich and diverse set of tools for installing a wheel that work cleanly inside of docker with very little work.

If there were just an _option_ to use the lockfile dependencies in the wheel, then poetry could remove the shackles of being a makeshift deployment tool.

But some of us do have a real requirement to ensure our docker images build exactly as we intended them to.

If you look through poetry issues, you'll find a good few people complaining that installing poetry in a docker image is complex and messy. _(though it has admittedly improved in versions between 1.1 to 1.3)_

### Closing remarks

I'd like to humbly suggest that poetry doesn't need to take any interest in building docker images into account.  This should not generally be supported.  There is a very rich and diverse set of tools for installing a wheel that work cleanly inside of docker with very little work.

If there were just an _option_ to use the lockfile dependencies in the wheel, then poetry could remove the shackles of being a makeshift deployment tool.
kept_issues.title: Option to use lockfile dependencies in wheel instead of pyproject.toml versions

## Feature Request

One of the cool features of pip is the ability to install dependencies without any internet/private pip repository access. This is a highly requested feature for isolated environments without any external access. 

How its works (basically):

###  Step 1. Vendoring dependencies (downloading deps locally)

```sh
mkdir vendor
pip download -r requirements.txt -d --platform manylinux1_x86_64 --python-version 3.9
git add ./vendor/*
```

###  Step 2. Installing dependencies from vendor

```sh
pip install -r -requirements.txt --find-links ./vendor/* --no-index
```


I think it is easy to add this feature to poetry. We already have lock file `poetry.lock` with the following package description:

```toml
[[package]]
name = "astor"
version = "0.8.1"
description = "Read/rewrite/write Python ASTs"
category = "dev"
optional = false
python-versions = "!=3.0.*,!=3.1.*,!=3.2.*,!=3.3.*,>=2.7"
files = [
    {file = "astor-0.8.1-py2.py3-none-any.whl", hash = "sha256:070a54e890cefb5b3739d19f30f5a5ec840ffc9c50ffa7d23cc9fc1a38ebbfc5"},
    {file = "astor-0.8.1.tar.gz", hash = "sha256:6a6effda93f4e1ce9f618779b2dd1d9d84f1e32812c23a29b3fff6fd7f63fa5e"},
]
```

So, we can add the new section to `pyproject.toml` to configure vendoring feature:

```toml
[tool.poetry.vendoring]
directory = "./vendor"
```

and then the following command:

```sh
poetry add astor
```

will add new entry to  `poetry.lock` 

```toml
[[package]]
name = "astor"
version = "0.8.1"
# ...
find-links="./vendor/ " # HERE IS PATH TO DEPS 
# ...
```

**and** downloads dependency tarball locally into `/vendor` directory to allow to use it during

```sh
poetry install
```
kept_issues.title: Add dependency vendoring mechanism

## Feature Request
Plugins are super useful and we're now using https://github.com/monim67/poetry-bumpversion in our projects to keep `__version__` in the code in sync with the version in `pyproject.toml`. This plugin is configured by simply adding 

```
[tool.poetry_bumpversion.file."your_package/__init__.py"]
```

However, if someone builds the project and doesn't have `bumpversion` installed as a plugin, that is silently ignored and `__version__` is not updated. We need a way to declare that building this project requires `bumpversion>=x.y.z` to keep builds reproducible and consistent.

Or maybe at least poetry could error if it sees a config section that doesn't correspond to core or a known plugin?

## Feature Request
<!-- Now feel free to write your issue, and please be as descriptive as possible! -->
<!-- Thanks again 🙌 ❤ -->

I have the following project structure:
```
.
├── my-app
│   ├── poetry.lock
│   └── pyproject.toml
└── my-lib
    └── pyproject.toml
```

`my-app` depends as a path dependency on local `my-lib`, which has some other dependencies.

Generally everything works great (🎉🎉🎉), _BUT_:

It's hard to create an optimal docker build process for it. Generally in docker you try to do "heavy things that change rarely" first (e.g. your dependencies), and layer "things that change often" (e.g. your code) on top. So in a simple case a Dockerfile with poetry could look something like:

```
COPY poetry.lock pyproject.toml ./        # this changes rarely
RUN poetry install --no-root              # this might take a long time, but that's ok, it's usually cached
COPY . ./                                 # this changes often
RUN poetry install --only-root            # this has to run almost every time, but it's ok because it's quick
```

In the above example I would love to be able to skip not only "root" but also the "local" dependencies. I could put them in a dependency group and something like `--without local`, but that would also (correctly and unsurprisingly) exclude the indirect dependencies.

You can imagine that my dependency tree looks something like:

```
my-app          (local code, changes often)
└─> my-lib      (local code, changes often)
    ├─> foo     (from registry, changes rarely, very big library)
    └─> bar     (from registry, changes rarely, very big library)
```

I want to install the heavy `foo` and `bar` first, and then my lightweight `my-*` in the next.

I don't expect that poetry would directly support this specific use-case, but it would be great if there was **a more flexible  "exclude" mechanism**, which allows to exclude specific packages (but not their dependencies)

Maybe something like `poetry install --skip <regexp>`.

Currently this can be done by `poetry export | grep <xyz> | pip install` chain, but having to escape from poetry install to pip just for this reason is very ugly.

 Feature Request
 
 

This is not really a technical feature, as much as it is more of process-related so to speak

 Motivation

I use poetry a lot, both for personal projects and for academic and industrial projects (i love the dependency management engine). 
However, I often encounter build problems that do not allow me to run simple projects that otherwise work with other package managers. This happens mostly when switching between minors, or sometimes even when switching between patches (breaking semver rules). See an example here: 7691.

This causes some pretty major inconsistencies, Which sometimes impact pipelines and workflows, to the point of making me reconsider using Poetry.

I often read nice explanations of why certain changes are made, in issues. I appreciate this and recognize that there must be a lot of work behind each decision, but all of this remains rather hidden from the user.

 Proposal

For the above reasons I propose that a section of the documentation be dedicated to bridging the python software engineering gap for the Poetry user. The tox FAQ goes in that direction.

This could consist of tutorials and/or practical examples to deal with individual typical build/install situations. 
An example of sections might be the following:
1. Little build theory: how to best use build requirements with poetry (perhaps give references to understand)
2. Use cases:
 - How to deal with an old standard package, like ex no-PEP-517 (this is not very helpful, since it's too hidden and small, but it's something. other examples 3433)
 - How to deal with a package that need to be built locally (see linux case)
 - ...

 Expected Outcome

I hope that the application of this proposal or similar, will result in significant time savings on both sides: poetry devs and poetry users; sometimes anticipating or extinguishing the possibility of error due to lack of knowledge that the average user does not have (and in my humble opinion is not due to have most of the time).

Thank you for your great work

poetry publish --repository target

 - something else?

## Feature Request
With pandas 2.0 also comes optional dependencies. However, I only sometimes need some of the extras, depending on the selected extras in my own project, to avoid bloating of the installation. For example, in my Poetry project I always need pandas, but only when my database extra is installed, the pandas SQL extra dependencies (postgresql, mysql, sql-other) should be installed.
I currently have not found a way to do this that the installed extra dependencies of a dependency can depend on the extra chosen for my own project.

I believe there are multiple ways of going about this, I have two suggestions below.

### Being able to label dependency specifications and use those in the extra specification
```toml
[tool.poetry]
name = "packagename"
version = "0.0.0"
description = "..."
authors = ["..."]
maintainers = ['...']
license = 'Apache 2.0'
readme = "README.md"
repository = 'https://github.com/...'

[tool.poetry.dependencies]
python = ">=3.9, <3.12"
pandas = { version = "^2.0.0"}
pandas = { version = "^2.0.0", extras = ["performance", "postgresql", "mysql", "sql-other"], label="pandas-databases", optional=true }


[tool.poetry.extras]
databases = [
    'SQLAlchemy',
    'pyodbc',
    'pandas-databases'
]
```

### Use a notation similar to pip in the extra specification, potentially with declaration of optional extras
```toml
[tool.poetry]
name = "packagename"
version = "0.0.0"
description = "..."
authors = ["..."]
maintainers = ['...']
license = 'Apache 2.0'
readme = "README.md"
repository = 'https://github.com/...'

[tool.poetry.dependencies]
python = ">=3.9, <3.12"
pandas = { version = "^2.0.0", optional_extras=["performance", "postgresql", "mysql", "sql-other"]}


[tool.poetry.extras]
databases = [
    'SQLAlchemy',
    'pyodbc',
    'pandas[performance,postgresql,mysql,sql-other]'
]
```

 Feature Request

Poetry by design includes in its lockfile every wheel matching the version requirements of a package. This is done regardless of the Python version requirement, and is generally fine when ran against pypi. However this results in a big performance penalty wen ran against a repository that does not expose package hashes (pytorch once again 👀 ), which results in Poetry downloading a lot of unnecessary wheels.

Suppose I specify python = "~3.11" as Python version and add torch==specific-version as a dependency from its public repository As the repository does not provide hashes, Poetry will (rightfully) download wheels to compute a hash on them. However, it does it regardless of the Python specification - i.e. not only cp311 wheels are downloaded, but also cp39, cp38, ... This becomes increasingly slow as new Python versions are released.

I'm wondering if Poetry would accept a PR where the inclusion of packages in the lockfile (and thus its download) is pre-filtered by filtering on the matching wheels, or if I'm missing something for which this can/should not be done. While I agree that the PyTorch team should improve its repository, I think it doesn't hurt for Poetry to stay on the safe side and exploit this performance improvement if possible (as from real world experience PyTorch is not the only repository that does not expose hashes unfortunately).

---
Related:

## Feature Request

It would be nice to be able to view all possible groups through the CLI through a command such as `poetry list --groups` as opposed to having to open the pyproject.toml file.

In addition to the above, if groups supported an additional property `description` it would make the output of the above recommended command easier for users to interpret by showing the purpose for the group.

An alternative and simpler solution could be to include what group dependencies are in when running `poetry show --with dev`. For example, the output could be:

```text
coverage       7.2.7     dev      Code coverage measurement for Python
````

### Example

In the pyproject.toml file I could have:

```toml
[tool.poetry.group.dev]
description = "Optional dev dependencies used for testing and linting code"
optional = true

[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies]
coverage = "7.2.7"
pytest = "7.4.0"
ruff = "0.0.272"
```

Using the CLI, I could run:

```bash
> poetry list --groups

Groups:

dev: Optional dev dependencies used for testing and linting code
    coverage = "7.2.7"
    pytest = "7.4.0"
    ruff = "0.0.272"
```

 Feature Request
 
 

BOM dependencies allow to depend on a specific project that would limit the dependencies on our own project. BOM dependencies do not act as transitive dependencies as they wouldn't be installed unless explicitly defined in our current project or in its resoled transitive dependencies. For that matter, it would behave a bit more like the constraint file from pip, but has to be pulled like a dependency instead of being directly fetch from an uri.

I had great hope when I saw the optional dependencies feature come out, as that could bring BOM like features in a very easy way to poetry. I see two ways of making it work using optional dependencies:

 resolve optional transitive dependencies
The idea would be that when resolving dependency version, the optional dependencies version rules defined in one of our project dependencies (our BOM dependency) would be checked to do the version resolution that will end up in the poetry.lock

In practice, that would mean in the BOM project we would define an optional group dependencies with all the version rules applicable. The in our project we would add a dependency on the first project, then the dependencies to all requirements for our project. The version could be as simple as '' if we delegate everything to the BOM, or we could add our own version rules which the resolver would need to solve like any regular transitive dependencies.

 

 resolve optional dependencies' dependencies
instead of having the BOM project define the optional block, it would be the project that would define it as optional. Thus all transitive dependencies from the bom project should be used in the project resolution, in the same way as directly written dependencies are taken into account in resolution as stated by the doc
> All dependencies must be compatible with each other across groups since they will be resolved regardless of whether they are required for installation or not

So in practice, the bom dependencies would only be a normal project defining requirements. and our project would define its own requirement as usual, but adding the constraint of the transitive dependency on the BOM project:

 
---
 I feel the first solution would better address the goal of BOM dependency, but the second one might be closer to be usable in poetry in the current state.

In the end that kind of feature would make it a lot easier to keep uniformized dependencies across multiple projects managed by the same teams. Would also allow defining a "good stack" for large framework (although not much an issue in python). It would also help conformity when dependencies have to be approved before being used in a company.

## Feature Request
<!-- Now feel free to write your issue, and please be as descriptive as possible! -->
<!-- Thanks again 🙌 ❤ -->

BOM dependencies allow to depend on a specific project that would limit the dependencies on our own project. BOM dependencies do not act as transitive dependencies as they wouldn't be installed unless explicitly defined in our current project or in its resoled transitive dependencies. For that matter, it would behave a bit more like the constraint file from pip, but has to be pulled like a dependency instead of being directly fetch from an uri.

I had great hope when I saw the optional dependencies feature come out, as that could bring BOM like features in a very easy way to poetry. I see two ways of making it work using optional dependencies:

### resolve optional transitive dependencies
The idea would be that when resolving dependency version, the optional dependencies version rules defined in one of our project dependencies (our BOM dependency) would be checked to do the version resolution that will end up in the poetry.lock

In practice, that would mean in the BOM project we would define an optional group dependencies with all the version rules applicable. The in our project we would add a dependency on the first project, then the dependencies to all requirements for our project. The version could be as simple as '*' if we delegate everything to the BOM, or we could add our own version rules which the resolver would need to solve like any regular transitive dependencies.

```
[tool.poetry]
name = "enteprise-bom"
version = "1.1"

[tool.poetry.group.bom]
optional = true

[tool.poetry.group.bom.dependencies]
dep1 = "^1"
dep2 = "2.3.1"
dep3 = "^1.4.0"
dep4 = "^4.2"


============
[tool.poetry]
name = "our-projet"

[tool.poetry.dependencies]
enteprise-bom = "1.1"
dep1 = "*"             # resolve to "^1"
dep2 = "^2.1.1"        # resolve to "2.3.1"
dep3 = "~1.5.0"        # resolve to "~1.5.0"
                       # dep4 is not installed
dep5 = "^2.1"          # dep5 is install like any regular dependencies
```

### resolve optional dependencies' dependencies
instead of having the BOM project define the optional block, it would be the project that would define it as optional. Thus all transitive dependencies from the bom project should be used in the project resolution, in the same way as directly written dependencies are taken into account in resolution as stated by the doc
> All dependencies must be compatible with each other across groups since they will be resolved regardless of whether they are required for installation or not

So in practice, the bom dependencies would only be a normal project defining requirements. and our project would define its own requirement as usual, but adding the constraint of the transitive dependency on the BOM project:

```
[tool.poetry]
name = "enteprise-bom"
version = "1.1"

[tool.poetry.dependencies]
dep1 = "^1"
dep2 = "2.3.1"
dep3 = "^1.4.0"
dep4 = "^4.2"


============
[tool.poetry]
name = "our-projet"

[tool.poetry.dependencies]
dep1 = "*"             # resolve to "^1"
dep2 = "^2.1.1"        # resolve to "2.3.1"
dep3 = "~1.5.0"        # resolve to "~1.5.0"
                       # dep4 is not installed
dep5 = "^2.1"          # dep5 is install like any regular dependencies


[tool.poetry.group.bom]
optional = true

[tool.poetry.group.bom.dependencies]
enteprise-bom = "1.1"
```
---
 I feel the first solution would better address the goal of BOM dependency, but the second one might be closer to be usable in poetry in the current state.

In the end that kind of feature would make it a lot easier to keep uniformized dependencies across multiple projects managed by the same teams. Would also allow defining a "good stack" for large framework (although not much an issue in python). It would also help conformity when dependencies have to be approved before being used in a company.

## Some Context

On July 17th, a lot of people woke up to find out that they could no longer install PyYAML. The problem ended up not being that cython 3.0 had been released with some breaking changes.

- PyYAML issue: https://github.com/yaml/pyyaml/issues/724 and workaround (updating `build-system.requires` to have `Cython<3.0`: https://github.com/yaml/pyyaml/commit/ae08bdc82b4ddfcd2b93c8aedcd1963766c3307d
- Cython release history: https://pypi.org/project/Cython/#history
  ![image](https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/assets/277474/66e05aed-fde8-4ce0-8bac-63f6c2a8a933)

This affected a number of macOS developers on my team. This surprised me at first, because we use poetry, and I thought that poetry would have ensured we always build PyYAML with the same, locked version of Cython. However, looking through our lockfiles, I guess that's not the case (I see no mention of Cython whatsoever). Given that "DETERMINISTIC BUILDS" is one of the headlines on https://python-poetry.org/, I figured this is something Poetry would like to do a better job with.

## Feature Request

I'd like poetry installs to be more reproducibe. If I was able to successfully run `poetry install` yesterday, I'd like today's `poetry install` to run using the *exact same* `build-system.requires` for all the packages I need to build.

### Misc Thoughts

I *guess* what's happening is that poetry just leaves the PEP-517 isolated builds entirely in pip's hands. That is, when pip tries to build a package with a `pyproject.toml` like this:

```
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools", "wheel", "Cython"]
```

pip just uses whatever the latest version of setuptools/wheel/Cython are available.

I don't know enough about pip to know if it even *has* a mechanism for to say "Hey, please do a PEP-517 isolated build, but for those `build-system.requires`, use these specific versions, thanks". If it doesn't, perhaps that's something upstream pip would be willing to add support for? (I'm happy to inquire over there if it's helpful.)

 Feature Request
Currently, poetry new allows specifying different layouts, like the src layout, which creates the src and tests directory, and adjusts the pyproject.toml to install packages from the src directory. This feature is really useful for new packages, but can't be used with an existing directory, like poetry init. Adding the option --src option (or other layout options if they exist) to init would solve this. Now there are use-cases where neither poetry new and poetry init suffice because they require manual work that normally poetry takes care of.

 use-case

 create a new git repository
 clone the repository
 create a new poetry package with the src layout.

If I want a source layout (and hence use --src and need to use poetry new), this means I have to:
 poetry new
 git init
 git remote add origin 
 git checkout origin/main
 git commit -a

in order to make sure poetry is the one making the new directories.
Or with poetry init , I can first clone the remote repo and then run poetry init, but now I need to manually make the tests and src directories and modify pyproject.toml to add from = . 

Its all totally doable manually, but in the spirit of There should be one-- and preferably only one --obvious way to do it. it seems unnecessary to have both new and init and then have features that are useful for both be exclusively to one or the other. Once layouts exist in init, the new command really doesn't seem necessary anymore.

 Context and problem description
I'm currently trying to improve the packaging and distribution of this Python package. Its exact usecase is not all that important, only that the GUI portion of the tool requires wxPython and that everything is built and distributed with Poetry (automated through Github Actions). 

This GUI toolkit wxPython is currently not available as a prebuilt wheel for (any) Linux distribution on PYPI which ultimately means that running pip install libretro-finder (i.e. installing the package in question) on Linux distributions kickstarts a build of wxPython from source. This takes >45 minutes on default Github Actions runners (ubuntu-latest) and requires a ton of system dependencies, both of which negatively impact the adoption rate among Linux users (if any) for what should ideally be a very simple tool.

The fine people over at wxPython do host a ton of prebuilt wheels for common Linux distributions on their own Apache file server (all of which appear to follow PEP427). It's just that it doesn't conform to PEP503 like PYPI does (if you can even say it like that) so Poetry can't accept it as a package source.

Sure, you can manually add one of the URLs as an explicit package source but that would ultimately mean only "supporting" the Linux distribution associated with that build (leaving other distros to build from source). It also hardcodes a package dependency and dramatically limits the value of poetry's lockfile (or that of a modern package manager in general).

 Feature Request

In short, it would be very useful if there was a way for Poetry to index arbitrary file servers (that host Python wheels) and ultimately accept them as package sources.

 Possible approach
At the risk of sounding naive, I currently imagine scraping an arbritrary file server to find all PEP427-conforming wheels and symlinking them to an in-memory representation of a Python package repository (index.html can then be computed with a templating engine). I then imagine dumping this to a versionable file and making it searchable by an API that follows PEP503 specs (at which point Poetry can accept it as a package source).

 Why this is useful
Besides my wxPython example, there are a ton of file stores (often from scientific/academic sources) that contain perfectly valid Python wheels that go unused simply because they're not available on PYPI. 
 
A simple way to index these packages locally and making them available again through a modern package manager can be quite valuable. Hell, renewed interest in these packages might even motivate the maintainers to finally make them properly available on PYPI (reaching here but who knows).

 What I've done, tried and considered (besides this FR)

For the sake of completion, here are the other solutions I've considered for my wxPython dependency issue (please comment if you have any other suggestions):

_- Moving the GUI dependencies of my package to extras and building two versions (libretro-finder and libretro-finder[gui])_
Practical for the people who just want the CLI but ultimately doesn't solve anything for the GUI version (I also don't really want to maintain two versions on all platforms).

_- Bundle all your binary dependencies and release your package as a conda package_
Would solve the issue for conda users but is just not as widespread as pip (which I assume that most casual users will still use)
 
_- Add every .whl URL as a separate (supplemental) source_
Would make the pyproject.toml very difficult to maintain since even a single package release can have ~5 versions.

_- Mirror the file server and make it PEP503 conformant yourself_
Someone actually already made a tool for this called simple503 but this assumes that you own the file server itself (or can otherwise configure it). Not only is that not the case for my wxPython example, mirroring a readily available source just to index them seems like a lot of effort if you consider the required infrastructure/memory costs. I still want this feature to download from the original host

_- Cache build artifacts_ 
Already implemented with Github Actions' actions/cache. Dramatically speeds up builds as wxPython no longer has to be rebuild if poetry.lock doesn't change. Doesn't solve anything for people installing libretro-finder through pip/poetry though (naturally).

 Continuation
First and foremost, I would love to hear you guys' thoughts on this and whether this is the right approach to take. I'm not completely sure if this actually aligns with the community's needs or whether it even fits within the scope of Poetry but curious to find that out.

Its exact usecase is not all that important, only that the GUI portion of the tool requires `wxPython` and that everything is built and distributed with Poetry ([automated through Github Actions](https://github.com/jaspersiebring/libretro_finder/blob/2b68fbd897edbca0405ac58e40e73c4b0ace4615/.github/workflows/main.yml)). 

This GUI toolkit `wxPython` is currently not available as a prebuilt wheel for (any) Linux distribution on PYPI which ultimately means that running `pip install libretro-finder` (i.e. installing the package in question) on Linux distributions kickstarts a build of `wxPython` from source. This takes >45 minutes on default Github Actions runners (ubuntu-latest) and requires a ton of system dependencies, both of which negatively impact the adoption rate among Linux users (if any) for what should ideally be a very simple tool.

The fine people over at [wxPython](https://wxpython.org/pages/downloads/) do host a ton of prebuilt wheels for common Linux distributions on their [own Apache file server](https://extras.wxpython.org/wxPython4/extras/linux/gtk3/) (all of which appear to follow PEP427). It's just that it doesn't conform to PEP503 like PYPI does (if you can even say it like that) so Poetry can't accept it as a [package source](https://python-poetry.org/docs/repositories/#supported-package-sources).

Sure, you can manually add one of the URLs as an explicit package source but that would ultimately mean only "supporting" the Linux distribution associated with that build (leaving other distros to build from source). It also hardcodes a package dependency and dramatically limits the value of poetry's lockfile (or that of a modern package manager in general).

## Feature Request

In short, it would be very useful if there was a way for Poetry to index arbitrary file servers (that host Python wheels) and ultimately accept them as package sources.

##### Possible approach
At the risk of sounding naive, I currently imagine scraping an arbritrary file server to find all PEP427-conforming wheels and symlinking them to an in-memory representation of a Python package repository (index.html can then be computed with a templating engine). I then imagine dumping this to a versionable file and making it searchable by an API that follows PEP503 specs (at which point Poetry can accept it as a package source).

##### Why this is useful
Besides my `wxPython` example, there are a ton of file stores (often from scientific/academic sources) that contain perfectly valid Python wheels that go unused simply because they're not available on PYPI. 
 
A simple way to index these packages **locally** and making them available again through a modern package manager can be quite valuable. Hell, renewed interest in these packages might even motivate the maintainers to finally make them properly available on PYPI (reaching here but who knows).

## What I've done, tried and considered (besides this FR)

For the sake of completion, here are the other solutions I've considered for my `wxPython` dependency issue (please comment if you have any other suggestions):

_- Moving the GUI dependencies of my package to `extras` and building two versions (libretro-finder and libretro-finder[gui])_
Practical for the people who just want the CLI but ultimately doesn't solve anything for the GUI version (I also don't really want to maintain two versions on all platforms).

_- Bundle all your binary dependencies and release your package as a conda package_
Would solve the issue for `conda` users but is just not as widespread as pip (which I assume that most casual users will still use)
 
_- Add every .whl URL as a separate (supplemental) source_
Would make the pyproject.toml very difficult to maintain since even a single package release can have ~5 versions.

_- Mirror the file server and make it PEP503 conformant yourself_
Someone actually already made a tool for this called [simple503](https://github.com/repo-helper/simple503) but this assumes that you own the file server itself (or can otherwise configure it). Not only is that not the case for my `wxPython` example, mirroring a readily available source just to index them seems like a lot of effort if you consider the required infrastructure/memory costs. I still want this feature to download from the original host

_- Cache build artifacts_ 
Already implemented with Github Actions' `actions/cache`. Dramatically speeds up builds as wxPython no longer has to be rebuild if poetry.lock doesn't change. Doesn't solve anything for people installing `libretro-finder` through `pip`/`poetry` though (naturally).

## Continuation
First and foremost, I would love to hear you guys' thoughts on this and whether this is the right approach to take. I'm not completely sure if this actually aligns with the community's needs or whether it even fits within the scope of Poetry but curious to find that out.
kept_issues.title: Ability for Poetry to index arbitrary (non-PEP503) file servers (that host Python wheels) and ultimately accepting them as package sources

kept_issues.body:
# Background

Python has historically used runtime functions like `ctypes.util.find_library` by invoking ldconfig and gcc to get the flags and libraries for native dependencies.

Not only that causes performance issues on startup, it's extremely inconvenient to provide such information at runtime
while it's a configure thing.

There are [tons of patches](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3ANixOS%2Fnixpkgs+ctypes.util.find_library&type=code) in nixpkgs to support this and most important, it makes the whole Python development experience on Nix(OS) unusable.

# Proposal

Support [pkgconfig](https://www.freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/pkg-config/) section in `pyproject.toml` itself, inspired by [autotools](https://autotools.info/pkgconfig/pkg_check_modules.html) interface.

```toml 
[tool.poetry.pkgconfig]
gtk-2.0 = {version = "^3.0", platform = "darwin"}
zlib = *
```

## Dependency alternatives

Sometimes there's a fallback to another library, so we can support that:

```toml
[tool.poetry.pkgconfig]
libsodium = {version = "*", alternative = "openssl" }
```

## Runtime querying

`importlib_metadata` would be extended with pkgconfig metadata.

## Open Questions

How to handle the cases where `pkg-config` is not available? See how that impacted [cabal](https://github.com/haskell/cabal/issues/7448) implementation.

cc @rgommers (packaging roundable discussion followup)
kept_issues.title: pkgconfig support

 Feature Request
 
 

 Summary
Configuration options to:
1. Reject usage of active venv (possibly with an option to override that behaviour through a command line option) AND/OR
2. Force creation of fresh isolated venv even if there is a venv already active (use active venv's base Python to create new venv)

 Motivation
Currently, even if virtualenvs.create is set to true, poetry will still use the active venv. This has undesired consequences:
1. poetry behavior is dependent on the environment it is running on (non-reproducible "builds")
2. leads to accidental installation of project dependencies into unrelated venvs.

Scenario when it is a problem: in organizations that have monolithic codebase and use plain pip, developers may rely on a single venv for the whole repository. This venv is often set as a global one (for example through pyenv global). With such setup it is very hard to incrementally introduce a tool like poetry without a coordinated effort. Poetry does not provide isolated environment and it's behavior may be accidentally influenced by the environment it is running in.

_Originally posted by @radoering in https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/issues/8376#issuecomment-1702981010_
            
I will prepare a PR to address this.

This affects wheel and sdist builds.
The related files MUST be added to the package. the files MUST NOT install on the host system.

well-known legal files are:
- LICENCE/LICENSE - obviously
- NOTICE - some license texts, like Apache-2.0, explicitly state this exact file (name) as a optional source of custom license addendum
- COPYING - obviously
- AUTHORS - obviously

read also: 
They describe this already, and they also allow arbitrary file suffixes.

 desired behavior 

- all the well-known legal files are detected automatically, and are added to be build result.
 - possibly arbitrary file suffixes are allowed
 - added to sdist root
 - added to wheel's .dist-info directory
- the bundled legal files are not "installed" during installation. they are not deflated into the site-packages

 current behavior 

with poetry 1.6.1:
- LICENSE is detected
- NOTICE is not detected
- COPYING is detected for wheel only
- AUTHORS is not detected

tried to add the needed files manually with include.

The related files MUST be added to the package. the files MUST NOT install on the host system.

well-known legal files are:
- `LICENCE`/`LICENSE` - obviously
- `NOTICE` - some license texts, like Apache-2.0, explicitly state this exact file (name) as a optional source of custom license addendum
- `COPYING` - obviously
- `AUTHORS` - obviously


read also: https://wheel.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user_guide.html?#including-license-files-in-the-generated-wheel-file
They describe this already, and they also allow arbitrary file suffixes.

### desired behavior 

- all the well-known legal files are detected automatically, and are added to be build result.
  - possibly arbitrary file suffixes are allowed
  - added to `sdist` root
  - added to `wheel`'s `.dist-info` directory
- the bundled legal files are not "installed" during installation. they are not deflated into the `site-packages`

### current behavior 


with poetry 1.6.1:
- `LICENSE` is detected
- `NOTICE` is not detected
- `COPYING` is detected for `wheel` only
- `AUTHORS` is not detected 


----

tried to add the needed files manually with [`include`](https://python-poetry.org/docs/pyproject#include-and-exclude).
This will also cause the files to be installed into `site-packages`, which MUST NOT happen.

----

found a feature request to have the list of `legal_files` configurable, which made it never to public.
But this issue is not about configuration but about auto-detect, one like other packaging systems have.
kept_issues.title: feat: add well-known legal files to build result automatically

Poetry should set its own user agent. Currently it makes all requests (both for package versions list retrieval and package download) with the default one provided by the `requests` library: `python-requests/<version>`, e.g. `python-requests/2.31.0`.

Lack of an unique user agent makes it tricky to differentiate between installer and human requests.

But there is another reason such a differentiation is useful - it makes it possible to show cached data to installers while avoiding stale results when traversed manually.

 Feature Request

 Motivation
Many company development ecosystems rely on libraries published to an internal package index, but also rely on libraries found on the public PyPI. 
This bears the potential for _name shadowing_, i.e. a package being published to PyPI that has the exact same name as a package of an internal registry. 
When name shadowing occurs, a dependency resolver may install a dependency from the public PyPI, even though the package from the internal registry was intended. 

Malicious actors can use this mechanism to inject malware onto target's machines, an attack known as a _dependency confusion attack_. Such attacks are becoming more popular, with an example being the attack on the popular machine learning framework PyTorch in January 2023 (link to a blog post I found). 

At my company, we are concerned about this threat, and have been thinking about ways to prevent this from happening to novice devs that are unaware of such threats. One option is to name-shadow the internal packages on PyPI ourselves, thus being in control of the name-shadowing packages. But this is not a responsible behavior, as it would result in dozens of empty packages on PyPI that simply exist to block the name. 

 Existing solutions in Poetry and their shortcomings
Poetry already has strong features for specifying dependency sources. 
Sources can have varying priority in Poetry (docs), and the source of packages can be specified explicitly (docs).
This goes a long way already. 

What is missing though, is a way to make Poetry enforce any measures described above, across projects.
Only through enforcing protective measures do they become reliable at a large scale. 
 
Two separate things could be enforced that would help here: 
1. The priority of PyPI could be enforced to be explicit.
2. Enforce a source specification on each dependency. 

Both options make each dependency on a public PyPI package a conscious decision, as it must specify source = "PyPI" to be installable. I prefer the second option, as it provides the additional benefit of reducing the network requests required to find a dependency. 

 Proposal
Enforcing the measures described above could be implemented as a Poetry configuration option (docs). 

In particular, I propose a boolean configuration option with a name such as dependencies.require_source that, when set to true, will validate dependency sources being specified on each command that involves adding, installing or updating dependencies.

## Feature Request

### Motivation
Many company development ecosystems rely on libraries published to an internal package index, but also rely on libraries found on the public PyPI. 
This bears the potential for _name shadowing_, i.e. a package being published to PyPI that has the exact same name as a package of an internal registry. 
When name shadowing occurs, a dependency resolver may install a dependency from the public PyPI, even though the package from the internal registry was intended. 

Malicious actors can use this mechanism to inject malware onto target's machines, an attack known as a _dependency confusion attack_. Such attacks are becoming more popular, with an example being the attack on the popular machine learning framework PyTorch in January 2023 (link to a [blog post](https://medium.com/checkmarx-security/py-torch-a-leading-ml-framework-was-poisoned-with-malicious-dependency-e30f88242964) I found). 

At my company, we are concerned about this threat, and have been thinking about ways to prevent this from happening to novice devs that are unaware of such threats. One option is to name-shadow the internal packages on PyPI ourselves, thus being in control of the name-shadowing packages. But this is not a responsible behavior, as it would result in dozens of empty packages on PyPI that simply exist to block the name. 

### Existing solutions in Poetry and their shortcomings
Poetry already has strong features for specifying dependency sources. 
Sources can have varying priority in Poetry ([docs](https://python-poetry.org/docs/repositories/#package-sources)), and the source of packages can be specified explicitly ([docs](https://python-poetry.org/docs/repositories/#package-source-constraint)).
This goes a long way already. 

What is missing though, is a way to make Poetry enforce any measures described above, across projects.
Only through enforcing protective measures do they become reliable at a large scale. 
 
Two separate things could be enforced that would help here: 
1. The priority of PyPI could be enforced to be `explicit`.
2. Enforce a `source` specification on each dependency. 

Both options make each dependency on a public PyPI package a conscious decision, as it must specify `source = "PyPI"` to be installable. I prefer the second option, as it provides the additional benefit of reducing the network requests required to find a dependency. 

### Proposal
Enforcing the measures described above could be implemented as a Poetry configuration option ([docs](https://python-poetry.org/docs/configuration/)). 

In particular, I propose a boolean configuration option with a name such as `dependencies.require_source` that, when set to true, will validate dependency sources being specified on each command that involves adding, installing or updating dependencies.

```poetry run start```

This contrast in command syntax between standard Python and Poetry can create a minor hurdle, especially for developers switching between different Python projects. To enhance the user experience and maintain consistency, I propose a feature that streamlines script execution in Poetry.

**Feature Proposal:**

I suggest modifying the script command in Poetry's `pyproject.toml` to implicitly check for the presence of a `__main__.py` file and execute the `main` function if it exists. The change in the `pyproject.toml` file would look like this:

```toml
[tool.poetry.scripts]
start = "package_name:main"
```

This would eliminate the need to explicitly specify the `__main__.py` file, aligning Poetry's behavior with Python's conventions. The proposed feature offers numerous benefits:

**Benefits:**

1. **Improved User Experience:** This change simplifies script execution within Poetry, making it more intuitive for both new and experienced users. Developers can transition seamlessly between standard Python projects and Poetry-managed ones.

2. **Reduced Cognitive Load:** Users no longer need to remember or specify the `__main__.py` file in the script command, reducing potential sources of error.

3. **Consistency with Python:** The proposed feature aligns Poetry's behavior with Python's established conventions, making it a more seamless part of the Python development ecosystem.

4. **Enhanced Developer Productivity:** By streamlining script execution, this feature contributes to a more efficient and productive development workflow.

**Conclusion:**

This feature request aims to enhance the user experience within Poetry by simplifying script execution. It aligns with Poetry's mission to make Python development more intuitive and efficient, reducing friction in the development process. By implementing this feature, Poetry can further establish itself as a user-centric tool that prioritizes the needs of Python developers.

I believe that this enhancement would be a valuable addition to Poetry, benefiting both new and existing users. I look forward to the consideration of this feature request and am willing to contribute to its development if required.

Thank you for your attention and dedication to improving Poetry.

Love,
Mahmoud

**Edit**: Apparently, after reading [`specifications/entry-points`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/entry-points/), if we rename the `__main__.py` file to `__init__.py`, we can import the function to invoke without specifying `__init__`. For instance, in our `pyproject.toml`, we can define the script entry point as follows:

```toml
[tool.poetry.scripts]
start = "package_name:main"
```

package structure:

```diff
├── package_name
-│   └── __main__.py
+│   └── __init__.py
└── pyproject.toml
```

## Feature Request
Several of my team's projects are structured as monorepos, but there are some awkward edge-cases that have arisen when using Poetry to manage dependencies in these packages. To give you an idea of the structure of a typical repository, it looks something like this. We generally use path dependencies to inter-link dependent packages. There are a few hitches with this structure though, and unfortunately it means we have to depend on wheel-files atm.
```md
python/
    package_a
    package_b
javascript
    webapp
```

### Invalid PEP440 Versions in CI (Azure Pipelines)
When building projects in CI, poetry will use temporary versions for path-based dependencies that are invalid, presumably because CI is operating with a detached head.

Local Form: `<version>+<branchname>.<hash>`
In CI: `<version>+.<hash>`

The CI form of the dynamic path-depenedency version is PEP440 non-compliant, which results in CI errors. Things work fine locally though.

### Conditional Path Dependencies
For libraries intended for publication, local path dependencies become problematic because they can't be swapped out when using `poetry build` to generate publication artifacts. It would be nice if `poetry build` could replace path dependencies with version numbers in the distributed pyproject.toml file. It would even be reasonable to make this explicitly configurable:

`package_b = { path = "../package-b", develop = True, published={version="^1.2.3} }`

## Feature Request
I'm updating a project to use poetry, and in my `pyproject.toml` file I previously had this:

```toml
[project]
license = { file = "LICENCE.txt" }
```

[Python Packaging User Guide supports this syntax for `license`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/declaring-project-metadata/#license):

> * [TOML](https://toml.io/) type: table
> * Corresponding [core metadata](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/core-metadata/#core-metadata) field: [License](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/core-metadata/#core-metadata-license)
> 
> The table may have one of two keys. The `file` key has a string value that is a file path relative to `pyproject.toml` to the file which contains the license for the project. Tools MUST assume the file’s encoding is UTF-8. The `text` key has a string value which is the license of the project. These keys are mutually exclusive, so a tool MUST raise an error if the metadata specifies both keys.

Following the poetry documentation, I have changed it to this:

```toml
[tool.poetry]
license = { file = "LICENCE.txt" }
```

When I run `poetry check`, however, I get the following error:

> The Poetry configuration is invalid:
>   - data.license must be string

As a workaround I can change it to this:

```toml
[tool.poetry]
license = "MIT"
```

From the perspective of a dev who is new to poetry, it would be nice if poetry supported the same format as the PyPA spec — or at least update the documentation to acknowledge the difference and explain why poetry doesn't follow the PyPA spec 😇

 Feature Request

 Problem

A notable thing missing from poetry.lock are build-systems used to build from sdists.

This is useful in efforts like poetry2nix that uses Poetry metadata.
Nix build environments are constructed in a much stricter way where we cannot dynamically install/load build-systems.
Currently users of this tool have to resort to manually adding overrides into Nix code to work around this missing metadata.

This issue has been reported many times over the years in various forms:
- 
- 

And has generally been a large source of maintenance that could be completely automated away.

Adding this metadata also has other uses such as building tools that can statically inspect the build-time dependency graph.

 Solution

One more possible entries in poetry.lock:
- build-system.requires

We only need to know build-system.requires & up front when constructing the build environment.
There is no need to add build-system.backend or build-system.backend-path.

The PyPi API does not have this metadata. It would need to be extracted from the sdist.

 Note

Do note that this is _not_ a suggestion to lock build systems, merely to add the contents of build-system.requires.

## Feature Request

### Problem

A notable thing missing from `poetry.lock` are build-systems used to build from sdists.

This is useful in efforts like [poetry2nix](https://github.com/nix-community/poetry2nix) that uses Poetry metadata.
Nix build environments are constructed in a much stricter way where we cannot dynamically install/load build-systems.
Currently users of this tool have to resort to manually adding overrides into Nix code to work around this missing metadata.

This issue has been reported many times over the years in various forms:
- https://github.com/nix-community/poetry2nix/issues/568
- https://github.com/nix-community/poetry2nix/issues/1435

And has generally been a large source of maintenance that could be completely automated away.

Adding this metadata also has other uses such as building tools that can statically inspect the build-time dependency graph.

### Solution

One more possible entries in `poetry.lock`:
- `build-system.requires`

We only need to know `build-system.requires` & up front when constructing the build environment.
There is no need to add `build-system.backend` or `build-system.backend-path`.

The PyPi API does not have this metadata. It would need to be extracted from the sdist.

### Note

Do note that this is _not_ a suggestion to lock build systems, merely to add the contents of `build-system.requires`.
kept_issues.title: Add build-system.requires to lock file

Right now, when I start a new project, I can choose a python version. Say I choose python ^3.12. Oh no! I just realized that triton and pytorch don't yet use python 3.12! No problem, I'll just downgrade my python version in my poetry pyproject.toml file. If I do that, then I get this error:

Current Python version (3.12) is not allowed by the project (3.11.5).

This is nonsense. Just downgrade the python version, treat it like any other library. I can solve the problem by deleting the directory and restarting the entire project, but that's just awful UX. 

Poetry creates a virtual environment for use when it is first run, and then that python version appears to be locked for all time and I'm having a hell of a time changing it. When people on my team are off by third digit version numbers (3.11.5 vs 3.11.6), well, that means that each of us have created incompatible python versions and we can't run each other's code.

Please, please, please, please, just allow poetry to treat python like any other library, like it does when the project is first created.

kept_issues.body:
I noticed that the undocumented `build.py` step is executed _after_ `tool.poetry.scripts`. This is bad if `build.py` is used to generate one of those scripts. My proposal is to run `build.py` _before_ `tool.poetry.scripts`.

### Example

`pyproject.toml`:
```toml
[tool.poetry]
name = "sample"
version = "0.1.0"
description = ""
authors = []

[tool.poetry.build]
generate-setup-file = true
script = "build.py"  # generates sample/sample_script

[tool.poetry.scripts]
generated_script = { reference = "sample/sample_script", type = "file" }

[build-system]
requires = ["poetry-core", "setuptools"]
build-backend = "poetry.core.masonry.api"

```

`build.py`:
```python
import os

def build(_setup_kwargs):
    script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(__file__))
    output_file = os.path.join(script_dir, 'sample/sample_script')
    with open(output_file, 'w') as stream:
        stream.write('#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho "Sample Script"\n')
    os.chmod(output_file, 0o755)
```

Current output:
```
tmp/sample$ poetry --version
Poetry (version 1.8.2)
tmp/sample$ mkdir -p sample
tmp/sample$ touch sample/__init__.py
tmp/sample$ poetry build
Preparing build environment with build-system requirements poetry-core, setuptools
Building sample (0.1.0)
  - Building sdist

/home/weisslj/tmp/sample/sample/sample_script in script specification (generated_script) is not found.
```

Expected output:
```
tmp/sample$ poetry --version
Poetry (version 1.8.2)
tmp/sample$ mkdir -p sample
tmp/sample$ touch sample/__init__.py
tmp/sample$ poetry build
Preparing build environment with build-system requirements poetry-core, setuptools
Building sample (0.1.0)
  - Building sdist
  - Built sample-0.1.0.tar.gz
  - Building wheel
running build
running build_py
creating /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build
creating /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/lib
creating /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/lib/sample
copying sample/__init__.py -> /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/lib/sample
copying sample/__init__.py -> /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/lib/sample
copying sample/sample_script -> /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/lib/sample
running build_scripts
creating /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/scripts-3.11
copying sample/sample_script -> /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/scripts-3.11
  - Built sample-0.1.0-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_36_x86_64.whl
```

The wheel should contain `sample_script` as script:
```
tmp/sample$ unzip -l dist/sample-0.1.0-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_36_x86_64.whl | grep sample_script
       41  1980-01-01 00:00   sample/sample_script
       41  1980-01-01 00:00   sample-0.1.0.data/scripts/sample_script
```

 Feature Request

Currently, poetry does not allow good practices while packaging data with python. In particular, poetry expects the data associated with python packages to live alongside the python source files themselves. Furthermore, poetry does not install data files in standard data locations, and instead installs them in unstable locations inside site-packages which render the data files to be unusable to non-python programs. 

In order to allow for good practices for data distribution, poetry should explicitly allow for a data_files like feature from setup-tools which allows installation to stable locations inside the target file-system.

## Feature Request

Currently, poetry does not allow good practices while packaging data with python. In particular, poetry expects the data associated with python packages to live alongside the python source files themselves. Furthermore, poetry does not install data files in standard data locations, and instead installs them in unstable locations inside `site-packages` which render the data files to be unusable to non-python programs. 

In order to allow for good practices for data distribution, poetry should explicitly allow for a `data_files` like feature from setup-tools which allows installation to stable locations inside the target file-system.

## Feature Request
The current logic for setting the same dependency in multiple groups (eg. by merging the keys) does not allow for overrides of the `source` value and thus breaks `path` (and presumably `git` / `url`) overrides.

### Current Behaviour
If we specify a standard dependency as follows:
```
[tool.poetry.dependencies]
common-code = { version = ">=1.0.0, <2.0.0" }
```
Then is is possible to merge in a path dependency at development time, to be able to iterate on library changes, with:
```
[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies]
common-code = { path = "../common", develop = True }
```
(so long as the path dependency is still within the `version` range, of course!)

If the former dependency is pulled from a non-default source, though, this no longer becomes possible:
```
[tool.poetry.dependencies]
common-code = { version = ">=1.0.0, <2.0.0", source = "private-index" }

[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies]
common-code = { path = "../common", develop = True }

[[tool.poetry.source]]
name = "private-index"
url = "SNIP"
priority = "explicit"  # same behaviour regardless of value here
```

This gives the following error when attempting to `poetry lock`:
```
Incompatible constraints in requirements of application-package (0.0.1):
common-code @ file:///home/kevin/src/REPO/common (1.1.4)
common-code (>=1.1.0,<2.0.0) ; source=private-index
```

It should be possible to override dependencies with explicit sources in the same way as those without.
kept_issues.title: Support `source` overrides when merging dependencies between groups

The purpose is for aesthetic purposes, but also for conformity with the way most common tools work.

As we see, It is exceedingly common to support several different file names, especially "hidden" filename syntax. So my feature suggestion is to support several file names option - this can be done similarly to other open source projects, with a hierarchy of options, so as not to break backwards compatibility:

kept_issues.body:
I think an option `poetry install --all-optional-groups` is needed.

## What is the use-case for this?

When you create a project with optional dependency groups, as detailed in the poetry documentation for [managing-dependencies](https://python-poetry.org/docs/master/managing-dependencies/#optional-groups), you need to know all optional groups when you want to do a full installation of the project.

```toml
[tool.poetry.group.tests]
optional = true

[tool.poetry.group.tests.dependencies]
pytest = "^8.0.0"
```

 Example where an `poetry install --all-optional-groups --all-extras` would be nice is a `devcontainer.json` setup:

```json
{
	"name": "Python & Poetry",
	"dockerComposeFile": [
		"../../docker-compose.yml",
		"./docker-compose.yml"
	],
	"service": "demo",
	"workspaceFolder": "/workspaces/${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}",
	"postCreateCommand": "poetry install --all-extras --with=dev,test",
```

As you see, I need to list all optional groups one-by-one. This makes it harder (impossible) for a team-wide generic setup across multiple projects. 

## Just some random thoughts...

A solution/workarround would be to not use the `optional` setting for groups, i.e., have all groups mandatory and use `poetry install --only=main` when it is important to only have the main group installed. But then, what is the point of tagging groups as optional?

Also to mention, the installation concept of "extras" has this `--all-extras` option. Wouldn't it even make more sense to have groups by default optional, as it is the case for extras?

## Misc...

I saw this other feature-request #8244, which addresses another "optional" concept, which is that of individual dependencies and not the groups.
kept_issues.title: Add an option --all-optional-groups to poetry install

kept_issues.body:
### Issue Kind

Change in current behaviour

### Description

If a project has a path-dependency with `develop=true`.
Using `poetry install` should install all dev-dependencies of that path-dependency.

### Impact

Let's use the following motivating example.
I am working on an application and a library that external developers can use to integrate with my app.

This results in the following directory structure.

```
.
├── awesome_app
│   └── __init__.py
├── awesome-lib
│   ├── awesome_lib
│   │   └── __init__.py
│   └── pyproject.toml
├── poetry.lock
└── pyproject.toml
```

The `./pyproject.toml` in the repo-root installs `awesome_lib` as a path-dependency. 
``` toml
awesome-lib = { path = "./awesome-lib", develop=true}
```
and `./awesome-lib/pyproject.toml` includes a few type-stubs as developer dependencies.
``` toml
[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies]
types-requests = "^2.31.0"
```

Executing `poetry install` does not install `types-requests`.
i

See this [repo](https://github.com/ErikDeSmedt/poetry-feature-request) for a minimal example

### Workarounds

The first work-around is to change the installation procedure.

```
> poetry install
> cd awesome-lib; poetry install
```

The other work-around is to copy all dev-dependencies from `./awesome-lib/pyproject.toml` to `./pyproject.toml`
kept_issues.title: Install dev-dependencies of `Path`-dependencies

kept_issues.body:
### Issue Kind

Change in current behaviour

### Description

I noticed that files that are generated by the undocumented build = "build.py" step are not included in the dist/ packages after "poetry build".

### Example

`pyproject.toml`:
```toml
[tool.poetry]
name = "sample"
version = "0.1.0"
description = ""
authors = []
build = "build.py"

[build-system]
requires = ["poetry-core", "setuptools"]
build-backend = "poetry.core.masonry.api"
```

`build.py`:
```python
import os

def build(_setup_kwargs):
    script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(__file__))
    output_file = os.path.join(script_dir, 'sample/sample_script')
    with open(output_file, 'w') as stream:
        stream.write('#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho "Sample Script"\n')
    os.chmod(output_file, 0o755)
```

Build output:
```
tmp/sample$ poetry --version
Poetry (version 1.3.2)
tmp/sample$ mkdir -p sample
tmp/sample$ touch sample/__init__.py
tmp/sample$ poetry build
Preparing build environment with build-system requirements poetry-core, setuptools
Building sample (0.1.0)
running build
running build_py
creating /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build
creating /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/lib
creating /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/lib/sample
copying sample/__init__.py -> /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/lib/sample
copying sample/__init__.py -> /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/lib/sample
copying sample/sample_script -> /home/weisslj/tmp/sample/build/lib/sample
```

Package does not contain `sample_script`:
```
tmp/sample$ unzip -l dist/sample-0.1.0-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_36_x86_64.whl 
Archive:  dist/sample-0.1.0-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_36_x86_64.whl
  Length      Date    Time    Name
---------  ---------- -----   ----
        0  1980-01-01 00:00   sample/__init__.py
      608  1980-01-01 00:00   sample-0.1.0.dist-info/METADATA
      110  1980-01-01 00:00   sample-0.1.0.dist-info/WHEEL
      275  2016-01-01 00:00   sample-0.1.0.dist-info/RECORD
---------                     -------
      993                     4 files
```

### Impact

Without this, I do not know how to include compiled files (e.g. Rust) in the Python package. This was previously reported in https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/issues/8856.

### Workarounds

A workaround is to call `poetry build` twice. Then:
```
tmp/sample$ unzip -l dist/sample-0.1.0-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_36_x86_64.whl 
Archive:  dist/sample-0.1.0-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_36_x86_64.whl
  Length      Date    Time    Name
---------  ---------- -----   ----
        0  1980-01-01 00:00   sample/__init__.py
       41  1980-01-01 00:00   sample/sample_script
      608  1980-01-01 00:00   sample-0.1.0.dist-info/METADATA
      110  1980-01-01 00:00   sample-0.1.0.dist-info/WHEEL
      350  2016-01-01 00:00   sample-0.1.0.dist-info/RECORD
---------                     -------
     1109                     5 files
```
kept_issues.title: Allow results from "build" step to be part of the package

In some of my projects, we decide to exclude the use of specific dependencies (i.e. pandas). Whilst it is easy to check during a code review if someone attempted to add it as a dependency by checking the pyproject.toml file, it isn't easy to know if pandas is a sub-dependency of another dependency.

kept_issues.body:
### Issue Kind

Brand new capability

### Description

Currently Poetry doesn't seem to be have a way to install packages with `--no-binary` flag. There were two previous issues that I could find about this: https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/issues/365 and https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/issues/1316 both were closed, not sure why. One of them mention the introduction of this option, but I don't seem to have it:

```shell
(.venv) user@imac ~/project (main*?) $ poetry add psycopg2 --no-binary

The option "--no-binary" does not exist
(.venv) user@imac ~/project (main*?) $ poetry add --no-binary psycopg2

The option "--no-binary" does not exist
```

In this specific case, it seems Homebrew changed the logic with postgres/libpq, so `psycopg2` needs to be reinstalled with `no-binary` for it to update the `libpq` path. At this moment there doesn't seem to be a way to do that using Poetry.

It seems I could potentially use the local config with `poetry config --local installer.no-binary all,psycopg2` which I also couldn't make it work. Not only that, it seems unexpected that what is a `pip`'s  installer flag has to be defined on the project configuration level.

### Impact

For this scenario specifically, psycopg needs to be installed with `no-binary` which means that not having this in `Poetry` makes it impossible to handle the package using Poetry only.

### Workarounds

Only workaround I could find was to fallback to an alternative package management tool `pip`:  `pip3 install --no-binary :all: psycopg2 --force-reinstall`. It is expected that the package management tool currently in use would handle that situation, rather than relying on a different tool.
kept_issues.title: Add `--no-binary` flag to `add` action

### Issue Kind

Brand new capability

### Description

I want to define an extra for my package that pins specific versions of some dependencies, without affecting dependency resolution when it is not used.

My use case: I'm writing a library that depends on [jax](https://github.com/google/jax). I want to define an extras `metal` that installs [jax-metal](https://pypi.org/project/jax-metal) to support Apple GPUs. However, `jax-metal` requires a specific version of `jaxlib`. Since `jax` updates frequently, it is limiting to force a certain version of `jax` even when the extra is not used.

Possible way the thing could look like:

```toml
[tool.poetry.dependencies]
jax = "^0.4.22"
jaxlib = "^0.4.22"
jax-metal = { version = "0.0.6", optional = true }

[tool.poetry.extras]
metal = [
    "jax-metal",
    { change-dependency = "jaxlib", version = "0.4.22" },
]
```

Would it be possible at all to do this? Or is it blocked by the way pip itself handles extras in packages it installs?

### Impact

I've found someone having a similar problem on [this stackoverflow thread](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/67476031/poetry-install-different-package-version-based-on-extras). They made a plugin, but 1) it seems unmaintained and a bit messy, so I don't trust depending on it, 2) it works at the level of installing groups, so not for the extras in my final released package.

I guess there are other people with similar needs, but I don't know how many.

### Workarounds

Workarounds I know of:

- Create a separate package for my library with different dependencies
    - Time-consuming for me
- Ask users to install jax-metal themselves following instructions
    - Time-consuming for users
    - Annoying for me because I can't use poetry to install things on my development copy
